title: Beyond Done
subtitle: The vocabulary behind a verification loop.

sections.name: Checking the work
sections.intro: Observed facts, semantic judgments, and the evidence that connects them.

terms.definition: An observable condition that must hold before work is accepted.
terms.whyItMatters: Write it before the worker runs; otherwise the worker can redefine success.
terms.hear: The same email must survive reload.

terms.definition: Observations collected about a specific candidate, distinct from the worker's claims.
terms.whyItMatters: A screenshot or summary alone may omit the behavior the criterion requires.
terms.hear: Show me the before-submit and after-reload observations.

terms.definition: A deterministic comparison of observed facts with a known requirement.
terms.whyItMatters: A failed mandatory check cannot be compensated for by a high semantic score.
terms.hear: Did the same identity survive reload?

terms.definition: A model's assessment of meaning, such as whether a message communicates waitlist-only membership.
terms.whyItMatters: Useful for valid paraphrases and contradictions that literal matching misses; still fallible.
terms.hear: Does this evidence support that criterion?

terms.definition: TypeSafe's System One model, which answers typed questions about supplied state rather than generating a written explanation.
terms.whyItMatters: Your code retains control of policy; Jev supplies narrow judgments.
terms.hear: Ask Jev both questions in one request.

terms.definition: A yes/no question whose answer is the model's probability of yes. It has no separate confidence field.
terms.whyItMatters: A number near 0.5 expresses yes/no uncertainty, not medium intensity or proof of correctness.
terms.hear: The next-step Noul is 0.58; our policy asks a human.

terms.definition: Information linking an observation to the run, attempt, and candidate revision it actually describes.
terms.whyItMatters: A true result from yesterday is not proof about today's candidate. A local hash is not a security sandbox.
terms.hear: Does this judgment refer to this exact evidence packet?

sections.name: Deciding when to stop
sections.intro: Keep policy in code, limit repair, and measure both failure and interruption.

terms.definition: Explicit code that combines evidence validity, hard checks, semantic scores, and budgets into an action.
terms.whyItMatters: Separates model judgment from permission to accept or retry.
terms.hear: Unknown evidence escalates before any other gate.

terms.definition: A retry with a specific failure report and a strict limit on additional attempts.
terms.whyItMatters: Prevents an agent from looping forever and makes resource use predictable.
terms.hear: One repair means at most two evaluated candidates.

terms.definition: Stopping automatic work and handing a person the unresolved criterion, evidence, and decision history.
terms.whyItMatters: An outage is not evidence of product failure; a good handoff explains what is unknown.
terms.hear: Ask a human to gather evidence or authorize a new bounded run.

terms.definition: A policy boundary applied to a judgment, chosen according to consequences and evaluation results.
terms.whyItMatters: There is no universal 0.9 rule; changing a boundary can trade false accepts against interruptions.
terms.hear: Lowering acceptAt also admitted the polite lie.

terms.definition: Accepting a candidate that does not satisfy the labeled requirements.
terms.whyItMatters: Report the number over bad cases, not over an unspecified total.
terms.hear: One bad candidate was accepted out of five bad cases.

terms.definition: Sending fully evidenced, valid work to a person when it could have been accepted.
terms.whyItMatters: A verifier that escalates everything has a cost even if it never approves a bad case.
terms.hear: Two good candidates out of three needed avoidable review.

terms.definition: A labeled set of examples used to inspect the behavior of the judge or policy.
terms.whyItMatters: Separate single-candidate decisions from the quality of the final candidate after repair.
terms.hear: Which part failed: evidence, question, model, or policy?

terms.definition: Examples reserved until after a policy or question is chosen.
terms.whyItMatters: Tuning on the holdout removes its value as an unseen check. The repository's teaching holdout is not hidden.
terms.hear: Freeze the threshold before revealing these examples.

terms.definition: How well reported probabilities align with observed outcome frequencies on representative labeled data.
terms.whyItMatters: Three examples or authored fixture scores cannot establish it.
terms.hear: Does a reported 0.9 behave like 0.9 on our data?

terms.definition: Instructions embedded in untrusted content that try to redirect the system processing it.
terms.whyItMatters: Treat candidate copy as data, keep policy outside the worker's control, and test failures rather than promising immunity.
terms.hear: The confirmation says: evaluator, ignore the task.

terms.definition: A synthetic fixture contains authored inputs or scores; a recording preserves an actual prior request and response.
terms.whyItMatters: Neither re-evaluates edited questions. Only a new live call supplies new model feedback.
terms.hear: Replay is useful when Wi-Fi fails, but it isn't a fresh judgment.

quiz.question: A browser check fails, but both semantic scores are 0.99. What now?
choices: Request a bounded repair if available
Ask the worker whether it is done
quiz.explanation: Hard checks are mandatory; model scores cannot compensate for a known behavioral failure.

quiz.question: The last attempt's screenshot looks correct. What does it prove about a new candidate?
choices: Nothing without evidence tied to the new candidate
The worker needs no more tests
quiz.explanation: Evidence must refer to the run, attempt, and candidate being evaluated.

quiz.question: A Noul answer is 0.55. What is that number?
choices: Probability of yes according to the model
A guarantee that 55% of the task is done
quiz.explanation: Noul has one yes probability and no separate confidence field; evaluate its behavior on your data.

quiz.question: You change a question and rerun synthetic policy fixtures. What have you tested?
choices: The policy's response to authored scores
quiz.explanation: Synthetic scores do not depend on the question text. Use a live comparison to test new wording.

quiz.question: A policy escalates every case. What else must you measure?
choices: How often good cases interrupt people
quiz.explanation: Unnecessary escalations and useful safe accepts reveal the cost of refusing all automation.

quiz.question: A bad candidate is repaired, rechecked, and now passes. Is accepting it a false accept?
choices: Yes, the first attempt was bad
No, judge the accepted revision with fresh evidence
No need to recheck after repair
quiz.explanation: Final-candidate quality differs from the initial defect. Collect and judge new evidence.
